extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and mathematicians seeking an overview of what constitutes a mathematical proof
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for producing or evaluating mathematical proofs: how proofs must be constructed, justified, and presented so they are accepted by the mathematical community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs establish certainty through exhaustive deductive reasoning, distinct from empirical or inductive arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid proof yields logical certainty rather than probabilistic or empirical support; it must use deduction so the conclusion follows necessarily from premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal truth (covers all cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof must demonstrate that the statement is true in all possible cases, not merely present supporting examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on examples, experiments, or finite verification. The argument must handle every instance in the stated domain (e.g., via case analysis, general argument, or induction that is itself deductive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous argumentation in natural language
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is expressed in natural language and is a rigorous argument intended to convince the audience of the truth of a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity and logical structure in exposition are required; the proof should be articulated in a way that makes the logical steps explicit enough to convince the intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community standards of rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: To gain acceptance, a proof has to meet communal standards of rigor; an argument considered vague or incomplete may be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor is socially calibrated — what counts as acceptable detail or formality depends on the audience (e.g., peers, journal referees). Provide the level of detail and justification expected by that community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom-based reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct proofs from axioms and accepted rules of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base arguments on the agreed axioms, definitions, and previously established theorems; make the use of foundational assumptions and inference rules clear where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive (not inductive) logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive, not inductive, reasoning establishes certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish deductive steps (which guarantee the conclusion given premises) from inductive or heuristic arguments (which do not). If using induction, ensure the inductive proof itself is deductively valid (base case plus valid inductive step).

rubrics_metrics.name: Encyclopedic summary criterion for a 'good' proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is 'good' iff it (i) is deductive, (ii) covers all cases, (iii) builds from axioms, (iv) is convincing to the relevant community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as an evaluative summary: ensure deductive structure, completeness over cases, axiomatic grounding, and conformity to the target community's expectations of rigor and exposition.
